title: American consumers face pitfalls with rise of 'buy now, pay later'
summary: Economics correspondent Paul Solman examines buy now, pay later, a form of instalment credit now used by tens of millions of Americans, increasingly for groceries, utilities and other necessities rather than splurges. Borrowers including a Wisconsin teacher and a woman whose husband was laid off describe small plans that quietly piled up into large debts, while the industry's trade group defends the interest-free four-payment plan as transparent and a source of flexibility for stretched households. A credit counsellor and a consumer-law advocate warn about embedded interest, fees and a slide toward payday and title loans, and Harvard economist David Laibson explains how present bias makes deferring the cost so tempting.
focus: Shadow the economist's short explanation of present bias with his everyday diet-and-exercise example, then the credit counsellor's brief exchange on why interest baked into the payments means paying early saves nothing; both are clear, well-paced explanatory passages.

vocab.meaning: spreading through every part of something; found everywhere
vocab.context: The reporter described pay-later plans as having spread into almost every corner of American shopping, from clothes to groceries.
vocab.example: Once a workaround becomes this pervasive across business units, it is no longer an exception but the real operating model.

vocab.meaning: an organisation that represents and lobbies for companies in one industry
vocab.context: The industry's representative spoke on behalf of the association that lobbies for the pay-later lenders.
vocab.example: The trade group is likely to push back hard on any rule that caps fees, so we should map its arguments before the regulator meets.

vocab.meaning: to proudly mention a fact that makes you or your organisation look good
vocab.context: The industry spokesperson proudly pointed to the fact that the basic four-payment plan charges no interest.
vocab.example: The target boasts a 40% repeat-purchase rate, but we need to check how much of that is driven by discounts.

vocab.meaning: a small, short-term loan with very high fees, meant to be repaid on the borrower's next payday
vocab.zh: 发薪日贷款（高息短期贷款）
vocab.context: The credit counsellor said many of his clients graduate from pay-later plans to these costly short-term loans.
vocab.example: Our survey shows that customers who miss two instalments are three times more likely to take out a payday loan.

vocab.meaning: a high-cost loan in which the borrower's car ownership document is used as security
vocab.context: These were named alongside payday loans as the next, more dangerous step for borrowers who are already stretched.
vocab.example: Any lender moving into title loans should expect heavy reputational scrutiny from consumer advocates.

vocab.meaning: to end someone's employment, usually because there is not enough work or money
vocab.context: One borrower explained that her money problems deepened after her husband lost his job.
vocab.example: The client plans to lay off 8% of its back-office staff once the automation programme goes live.

vocab.meaning: something that helps a person or organisation survive a very difficult period
vocab.context: The industry argued that flexible instalments give households in tough times a way to cover essentials.
vocab.example: For many small suppliers, early-payment financing from the anchor customer is a lifeline during the slow season.

vocab.meaning: something that rescues you from a difficult situation just when you need it
vocab.context: A user described the service as having rescued her at moments when she could not cover a bill.
vocab.example: The shared-services dashboard was a lifesaver during the close; it cut reconciliation time in half.

vocab.meaning: the tendency to give too much weight to rewards now and too little to costs in the future
vocab.zh: 现时偏差（偏重眼前利益）
vocab.context: A Harvard economist used this concept to explain why spreading payments into the future feels so attractive.
vocab.example: Present bias explains why employees under-save, so the default enrolment rate matters more than the match.

vocab.context: The reporter used the image of protection to ask how consumers could defend themselves against products that play on their weaknesses.
vocab.example: A strong balance sheet is the best armour against an activist investor in a downturn.

vocab.meaning: to announce or advertise something loudly and proudly
vocab.context: The reporter noted that certain costs of the plans are not exactly advertised loudly to customers.
vocab.example: The company trumpeted its AI partnership in the press release but said nothing about the margin impact.

vocab.meaning: a charge you must pay when a payment is made after the due date
vocab.context: Penalties for missed due dates were discussed as one way that small plans can become expensive.
vocab.example: Late fees currently make up 12% of the unit's revenue, which is a regulatory risk we should flag to the board.

vocab.meaning: included from the start as part of a price, plan or system
vocab.context: The counsellor explained that the cost of borrowing is already included in each monthly payment, so paying early saves nothing.
vocab.example: Make sure the inflation assumption is built into the base case rather than added as a separate scenario.

phrases.meaning: to have just enough money to pay for the things you need
phrases.zh: 勉强维持生计；收支相抵
phrases.context: A survey figure showed that more than half of users say they could not cover their basic costs without these plans.
phrases.example: With wages flat and rents rising, many frontline staff are struggling to make ends meet, which is driving turnover.

phrases.meaning: to earn or find enough money to feed your family and cover basic needs
phrases.context: A teacher explained that she used the plans for everyday necessities just to keep her household going.
phrases.example: For gig workers, the platform's weekly payout is what keeps food on the table, so any delay hits loyalty hard.

phrases.meaning: (of a problem) to grow gradually without you noticing until it is serious
phrases.zh: 不知不觉地逼近；悄悄累积
phrases.context: Borrowers described how the debt built up quietly until the total surprised them.
phrases.example: Technical debt tends to sneak up on fast-growing firms until a single outage exposes it.

phrases.meaning: to move something, such as a purchase or event, to an earlier time
phrases.context: The economist explained that these products let people bring a pleasure into the present while pushing the cost later.
phrases.example: Tariff fears caused retailers to pull forward orders into the third quarter, flattering those numbers.

phrases.meaning: to combine into a total, often a surprisingly large one
phrases.context: One user described how many small instalments had gradually combined into a five-figure total.
phrases.example: Individually these discounts look small, but across the portfolio they add up to almost $30 million a year.
